questions.prompt: In this course's terms, what does it mean for Apex code to run "asynchronously"?
options: The code is handed off to the platform to run later, in its own transaction, without the caller waiting for it to finish
The code runs immediately in the calling transaction while the caller waits for it to finish
The code only runs if a human manually approves it from Setup
The code runs twice as fast as synchronous code by using more CPU threads
questions.explain: Asynchronous Apex hands work off to the platform to run later in its own transaction, with fresh governor limits, while the calling transaction finishes without waiting for it.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes synchronous execution, the opposite of asynchronous — it's the caller waiting on the spot, in the same transaction, that defines synchronous execution, not asynchronous.

questions.prompt: A process attempts to insert a GroupMember record and update an Account record in the same transaction. What happens, and why?
options: It throws a mixed DML error, because Salesforce doesn't allow DML on a setup object (GroupMember) and a non-setup object (Account) in the same transaction
It succeeds without issue, since GroupMember and Account are both standard objects
It throws an error only if the Account has more than 50 related records
It succeeds, but only if the running user is a System Administrator
questions.explain: Salesforce classifies GroupMember as a setup object. Combining DML on a setup object with DML on a non-setup object like Account in one transaction throws a mixed DML error — one of the concrete reasons asynchronous Apex exists.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a valid @future method signature?
options: public static void syncAccounts(Set<Id> accountIds)
public void syncAccounts(Account acc)
public static Account syncAccounts(Id accountId)
private static void syncAccounts(List<Account> accounts)
questions.explain: A future method must be static and return void, and its parameters must be primitives, arrays of primitives, or collections of primitives — a Set<Id> satisfies all three rules, unlike the other options, which either aren't static, return a non-void type, or take an sObject parameter.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a single Apex invocation can queue a maximum of ________ future method calls.
questions.explain: A single Apex invocation can queue a maximum of 50 future method calls, drawing from the same shared daily asynchronous Apex limit as every other async tool.

questions.prompt: Why can a Queueable job's constructor accept a List<Account> directly, something a future method's parameters cannot do?
options: A Queueable instance is serialized as a whole object, so it can carry sObjects and other non-primitive types directly
Queueable Apex doesn't actually enforce any governor limits at all
List<Account> is secretly treated as a primitive type by the Apex compiler
Future methods can accept List<Account> too; this is a common misconception the course corrects
questions.explain: Because a Queueable instance is serialized whole rather than passed as individual primitive arguments, it can carry real sObjects and custom Apex classes directly — one of Queueable Apex's clear advantages over future methods.

questions.prompt: Match each asynchronous Apex interface to the method(s) it requires you to implement.
right: No method of its own — it's a marker interface added alongside Queueable (or Batchable) to allow callouts
questions.explain: Queueable requires execute(QueueableContext). Database.Batchable<sObject> requires start, execute, and finish. Schedulable requires execute(SchedulableContext). Database.AllowsCallouts is a marker interface with no method of its own — it's added alongside Queueable or Batchable specifically to permit callouts.

questions.prompt: Put these three Batch Apex methods in the order the platform actually calls them when a batch job runs.
items: start — collects the records to process, called once
execute — processes one chunk of records, called once per chunk
finish — runs cleanup or sends a summary, called once after all chunks complete
questions.explain: Batch Apex always runs start once to collect records, then execute repeatedly (once per chunk, each its own transaction), and finally finish exactly once after every chunk has completed.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a Salesforce CRON expression has ________ fields, the last of which is optional.
questions.explain: A Salesforce CRON expression has seven fields — seconds, minutes, hours, day of month, month, day of week, and an optional year.

questions.prompt: What is the default maximum chain-depth stack for Queueable jobs in a Developer Edition or Trial org?
options: There is no limit in any org type
questions.explain: Developer Edition and Trial orgs default to a maximum stack depth of 5 — the original job plus four chained re-queues — though Salesforce's documentation notes this default can be overridden for specific use cases. Production orgs have no equivalent hard-enforced depth limit by default.

questions.prompt: What does Database.Stateful do when added to a Batch Apex class's declaration?
options: It preserves instance member variables' values across all of the job's chunk transactions
It allows the batch class to make HTTP callouts from execute
It changes the default chunk size from 200 to 2,000
It forces every chunk's execute call to share one single transaction
It lets start return an Iterable instead of a Database.QueryLocator
It automatically emails a summary to the org's admin when the job finishes
questions.explain: Database.Stateful is a marker interface that preserves a Batch Apex class's instance member variables across every chunk transaction, which is otherwise stateless by default.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes Database.AllowsCallouts, not Database.Stateful — callout permission and state preservation are two entirely separate interfaces with separate purposes. Database.Stateful only preserves instance member variable values across chunks; it has nothing to do with permitting callouts.

questions.prompt: Match each Setup monitoring page to the system object that actually underlies it.
questions.explain: The Apex Jobs page is a UI over AsyncApexJob, tracking future, Queueable, and Batch Apex runs. The Scheduled Jobs page is a UI over CronTrigger (linked to CronJobDetail), tracking registered CRON jobs and their next fire time.

questions.prompt: Why does wrapping each record's processing in its own try/catch inside a Batch Apex execute method (rather than one try/catch around the whole chunk) matter?
options: It has no real effect — a single chunk-wide try/catch behaves identically
A single bad record doesn't block the rest of the chunk from being processed; the loop continues and only the failed record is skipped and logged
It's required syntax for Database.Batchable to compile
It prevents the chunk from creating an AsyncApexJob record
questions.explain: Per-record try/catch means one failing record doesn't abort the whole chunk — the loop keeps going, and only the specific record that failed gets logged and excluded, while the rest of the chunk's work still completes.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the shared daily limit on asynchronous Apex executions is ________ per 24-hour period, or the org's user licenses multiplied by 200, whichever is greater.
questions.explain: The shared daily limit across all asynchronous Apex (future methods, Queueable, Batch Apex, and Scheduled Apex combined) is 250,000 executions per 24 hours, or licenses times 200, whichever is greater.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about per-transaction governor limits in asynchronous vs. synchronous Apex.
options: The SOQL query limit is higher in an asynchronous transaction (200) than a synchronous one (100)
The heap size limit is higher in an asynchronous transaction (12 MB) than a synchronous one (6 MB)
The DML statement limit is higher in an asynchronous transaction than a synchronous one
The total records retrieved by a single SOQL query (50,000) is the same in both synchronous and asynchronous contexts
Callout limits are completely removed in an asynchronous context, with no cap at all
questions.explain: SOQL queries and heap size are both doubled for asynchronous Apex (200 queries / 12 MB vs. 100 queries / 6 MB). DML statement limits (150) and total SOQL records retrieved (50,000) stay the same between the two contexts — asynchronous Apex gives more room on some limits, not unlimited room on all of them, and callouts still cap at 100 per transaction with a 120-second cumulative timeout.

questions.prompt: A requirement needs a job to run every night and touch millions of records. Per this course's decision framework, what's the typical design?
options: Scheduled Apex registers the nightly run, and its execute method calls Database.executeBatch on a Batch Apex class that does the actual processing in chunks
A single future method call handles all of the records directly
Queueable Apex alone, chained once per record
This can only be solved with a synchronous trigger
questions.explain: This is the classic 'Scheduled Apex triggers Batch Apex' pattern: the schedule decides when the job runs, and Batch Apex's chunked transactions handle the large record volume that a future method or a single synchronous transaction couldn't.

questions.prompt: In the StaleLeadCleanupBatch lab, why does execute call Database.update(toUpdate, false) instead of a plain update toUpdate; statement?
options: Passing false allows partial success — some Leads in the chunk can succeed even if others fail, instead of one bad record rolling back the whole chunk's DML
false tells Salesforce to skip all validation rules for every record in the list
There's no actual difference between the two forms of the statement
false converts the operation from an update into an upsert
questions.explain: Database.update(list, false) sets 'all or nothing' to false, so some records can succeed while others fail — the batch-level equivalent of per-record error handling, keeping one bad record from rolling back the entire chunk.

questions.prompt: Why does the nightly Account sync lab use Queueable Apex, implementing Database.AllowsCallouts, rather than Batch Apex for the actual sync work?
options: The nightly volume is small and bounded, and the job needs an HTTP callout plus job tracking — exactly the profile this course's framework matches to Queueable Apex rather than Batch Apex's large-volume use case
Batch Apex cannot be triggered by Scheduled Apex under any circumstances
Queueable Apex is required whenever a CRON expression is involved
Database.AllowsCallouts can only be implemented alongside Queueable, never alongside Database.Batchable
questions.explain: The sync only touches a few hundred Accounts a night (not batch-scale volume) but needs a callout and a trackable outcome — the exact profile this course's decision framework (Lesson 12) matches to Queueable Apex rather than Batch Apex.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about testing asynchronous Apex.
options: Work queued between Test.startTest() and Test.stopTest() runs synchronously at the moment Test.stopTest() is called
System.enqueueJob returns null when called inside a running test
A Queueable job's chain call should check Test.isRunningTest() to avoid an error when running inside a test
Scheduled Apex tests should assert on AsyncApexJob.NumberOfErrors immediately after calling System.schedule
Work already queued before Test.startTest() is flushed and executed when Test.stopTest() is called
questions.explain: Test.startTest()/Test.stopTest() runs queued async work synchronously at stopTest(), but only work queued inside that block — work queued before startTest() isn't flushed by it. System.enqueueJob returns null in test context, and chained Queueable calls need a Test.isRunningTest() guard to avoid an error. Scheduled Apex tests are better verified by asserting against CronTrigger's registered CronExpression, not by checking AsyncApexJob.NumberOfErrors right after scheduling.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the nightly Account sync design in the order they actually happen.
items: System.schedule registers NightlyAccountSyncSchedule against a nightly CRON expression
At the scheduled time, NightlyAccountSyncSchedule's execute method runs and calls System.enqueueJob
AccountNightlySyncJob's execute method queries flagged Accounts and sends an HTTP callout for each one
On a successful response, Needs_External_Sync__c is cleared; on failure, the flag is left set for the next night's run
questions.explain: The design runs in this order: the schedule is registered once, then at the scheduled time the Schedulable's execute enqueues the Queueable job, which does the actual callout work, and finally each Account's outcome determines whether its sync flag is cleared or left for a retry on the next run.

questions.prompt: A proposed design has a future method that takes the full Contact sObject as a parameter to sync to an external system. Running this through the design-review checklist reveals what?
options: The design won't compile as described, since future methods can't accept sObject parameters — it should pass the Contact's Id and re-query inside the method, or switch to Queueable Apex to accept the sObject directly
The design is already correct and needs no changes
The only problem is the method is missing the Database.Stateful interface
The design is fine as long as the org has fewer than 50 Contacts
questions.explain: Future methods only accept primitives, arrays of primitives, or collections of primitives — a Contact sObject parameter won't compile. The design-review checklist catches this immediately and points toward either passing the Id and re-querying, or switching to Queueable Apex, which can accept the sObject directly.
